summary: This work demonstrates a real-time adaptive feedback protocol for operating a superconducting transmon qubit that exhibits bistable frequency switching induced by a strongly coupled TLS defect. The 1-bit feedback scheme estimates which of two qubit frequency modes is active from a single optimally-timed measurement ($\tau_{\mathrm{opt}} \approx 1.33$ µs), then updates the control frequency accordingly to suppress dephasing and stabilize gate fidelities.
motivation: Parasitic TLS defects in dielectrics of superconducting qubits cause telegraphic frequency fluctuations that degrade coherence and gate fidelity. While ensemble TLS noise has been addressed, strongly coupled individual TLSs inducing discrete bistable frequency shifts require active mitigation strategies that operate on the qubit coherence timescale.
method: A TLS-syndrome circuit prepares the qubit in a superposition state calibrated for the high-frequency mode, evolves it for time $\tau_{\mathrm{opt}} = 1/(2\Delta_{\mathrm{TLS}})$ where $\Delta_{\mathrm{TLS}} \approx 374$ kHz, then applies an inverse pulse and measures in the Z basis. The single measurement outcome determines which mode is active; an FPGA-based controller (Quantum Machines OPX1000) uses this 1-bit feedback to update the drive frequency in real time with $\approx 136$ kHz bandwidth.
result: Randomized benchmarking over 14 minutes shows native single-qubit gate infidelity reduces from $(1.4 \pm 1.1) \times 10^{-3}$ without feedback to $(0.65 \pm 0.18) \times 10^{-3}$ with feedback—a 77% error reduction—while suppressing TLS-induced Ramsey beating. The estimation error probability is $p_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 9\%$, well below the 25% utility threshold.
